Agentic Work.note: A platform pillar spanning Genie and Agent Bricks, not a single product. Genie has no seat pricing; each user gets up to 10 US dollars of free monthly usage and you pay only for AI consumed beyond that.

Open Infrastructure.note: The open core: Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, Apache Spark and open Unity Catalog. Managed Iceberg tables in Unity Catalog are writable, but foreign Iceberg tables owned by an external catalog are read-only.

Ingest.note: An architecture stage, not one product: Lakeflow Connect, Auto Loader and Zerobus. Lakeflow Connect managed connectors run only on serverless compute and Lakeflow pipelines, and connectors sit at different release states.

Serve.note: An architecture stage covering BI, sharing, apps and APIs, not one product. Every path out inherits the caller's Unity Catalog permissions, so governance decides what each consumer can read.

Genie Agents & Business Use Cases.note: This band names what the platform is used for. Genie agent answer quality depends on the datasets, sample queries and instructions you curate for each agent, so setup effort matters more than model choice.

Cloud Services & Integrations.note: The cloud your workspace runs in and the outside systems it connects to. Classic compute runs in your own cloud account; serverless runs in the Databricks account, so 'your data stays in your perimeter' is fully true only for classic compute.

Sources.note: An architecture grouping of upstream systems, not a Databricks product. Access runs through Unity Catalog connections and storage credentials, and federated sources are queried in place rather than copied.

Consumers.note: An architecture grouping of downstream readers, not a product. Each consumer inherits the caller's Unity Catalog grants, so what a report, app or agent can read is decided by governance, not by the tool.

demos.t: Experience Databricks One: Empower Every Business User

External Ingestion.note: A grouping of non-Databricks pipelines (cloud ETL and third-party ELT), not one product. Partner ELT is billed separately per connector or row, and Lakeflow Connect now offers managed connectors for many of the same sources.

videos.t: Foundations of Data Teams

Teams.note: An architecture grouping of the people who use Databricks (business and technical), not a product or governed object. Real access is managed through Unity Catalog groups synced from your identity provider.

AWS DMS.note: Lands database change data as files in S3 that Databricks picks up with Auto Loader; ordering depends on the DMS commit timestamp columns.

AWS Glue.note: Existing Glue ETL jobs usually stay in place and write to S3, with Databricks reading those outputs as external or converted Delta tables.

AWS Glue Catalog.note: Federate it into Unity Catalog for read-only access to existing Glue tables; the connection needs IAM permissions on both Glue and the underlying S3 paths.

AWS IoT Core.note: Device messages are routed by IoT rules into Kinesis, MSK, or S3, and Databricks consumes that intermediate stream rather than IoT Core directly.

AWS KMS.note: Supplies customer-managed keys for workspace storage and managed services; the key policy must grant the Databricks control plane account access.

Agent Bricks.note: The code-first agent developer platform: bring any framework and model, deploy on Agent Runtime and use managed memory, tools and MLflow tracing. Knowledge Assistant and Supervisor Agent are legacy; build new low-code agents with Genie Agents.

Amazon Bedrock.note: Register Bedrock models as external model endpoints so calls are governed, logged, and billed through Unity Gateway alongside native models.

Amazon Kinesis / MSK.note: Kinesis is read by the native Structured Streaming source; MSK uses the Kafka connector with IAM or SASL authentication.

Amazon RDS / Aurora.note: Operational databases read by federation or CDC ingestion; Aurora PostgreSQL and MySQL use the same connectors as their RDS equivalents.

Amazon Redshift.note: Query it in place with Lakehouse Federation during migration; pushdown is limited, so large joins pull data across the network.

Amazon S3.note: Holds all table data; access runs through a Unity Catalog storage credential backed by an IAM role, not through instance profiles.

Anthropic / OpenAI.note: Anthropic Claude and OpenAI GPT are registered as external model endpoints and queried through Unity Gateway, so prompts and responses stay inside the workspace governance, spend-cap and logging path like any other model.

Azure Data Factory.note: Orchestrates Databricks notebook, jar and Jobs activities via a linked service; each activity can spin up a job cluster, so reuse pools to control cost.

Azure DevOps.note: Runs pipelines that deploy Declarative Automation Bundles (formerly Databricks Asset Bundles); the service connection needs a service principal, not a personal access token.

Azure Event Hubs.note: Consumed with the Structured Streaming Kafka connector against the Kafka-compatible endpoint, which requires the Standard tier or above.

Azure IoT Hub.note: Device ingestion front end; Databricks reads it through its built-in Event Hubs compatible endpoint rather than a dedicated connector.

Azure Key Vault.note: Backs Databricks secret scopes so credentials stay out of notebooks; the scope is read-only and secrets are managed in the vault.

Azure Monitor.note: Collects Databricks diagnostic logs and cluster metrics into Log Analytics; diagnostic settings must be enabled per workspace.

Azure SQL Database.note: Source for CDC ingestion or federated queries; needs firewall or private endpoint access from the Databricks VNet and a stored credential.

Azure Synapse.note: Read Synapse dedicated SQL pool tables through Lakehouse Federation, or migrate them; the old Synapse connector using PolyBase staging is deprecated.

BigQuery.note: Query it without copying via Lakehouse Federation; the service account needs BigQuery read session and job creation permissions in the source project.

Bronze.note: A layering convention with no platform enforcement. You implement it through pipelines and naming, and Unity Catalog does not validate or police layer boundaries.

Cloud Build.note: Runs the Databricks CLI to validate and deploy Declarative Automation Bundles (formerly Asset Bundles); the build service account needs a Databricks service principal token.

Cloud Data Fusion.note: Visual ingestion tool built on CDAP that typically lands data in Cloud Storage or BigQuery for Databricks to read downstream.

Cloud Identity.note: Google Workspace and Cloud Identity users authenticate to Databricks on Google Cloud through Google sign-in, with groups synced for entitlements.

Cloud KMS.note: Provides customer-managed encryption keys for workspace storage and managed services; check the customer-managed keys page for which resources are covered.

Cloud Logging.note: Receives platform and cluster logs for the workspace project; Databricks audit and usage data is exposed separately through system tables.

Cloud SQL.note: Operational PostgreSQL or MySQL source; federation needs network reachability from the Databricks VPC, usually private IP with peering.

Cloud SQL / Bigtable.note: Serving stores for curated output; Cloud SQL fits relational application queries while Bigtable fits wide-column lookups at high volume.

Cloud Storage.note: Primary table storage; Unity Catalog external locations use a Databricks-generated service account that must be granted bucket level roles.

CloudWatch.note: Collects cluster and job logs shipped from compute; Databricks system tables cover usage and audit data that CloudWatch does not.

CodePipeline / GitHub.note: Deploys Declarative Automation Bundles (formerly Databricks Asset Bundles) from source control; most teams use GitHub Actions for the same job with the Databricks CLI.

Fabric Data Factory.note: The pipeline and dataflow experience inside Fabric, separate from Azure Data Factory; used to move data between Fabric OneLake and other systems.

Teams & M365 Copilot.note: Account admins must enable the Genie app for Teams; channel replies are visible to everyone in the channel unless an admin restricts it to direct messages.

Notebooks & IDEs.note: Databricks Connect replaces the local Spark session so code runs remotely; the client Python minor version must match the cluster runtime or the session fails to start.

Operational APIs.note: The Statement Execution API runs on a SQL warehouse and carries result-size and wait-timeout limits, so high-QPS low-latency app serving usually needs Lakebase instead.

Reverse ETL.note: Sync frequency is bounded by the destination SaaS API rate limits rather than by Databricks compute, so very frequent syncs hit the CRM or ad platform first.

3rd Party CDPs.note: Databricks ships no packaged CDP; identity resolution, audience building and activation come from partner tools reading lakehouse tables you have to model yourself.

3rd-Party Marketplaces.note: External marketplaces normally deliver a physical copy into your own storage, whereas consuming from Databricks on a non-Databricks platform is limited to tabular data.

Marketplace Listings.note: Public listings require approval through the Databricks Data Partner Program and a Premium-or-above account; volumes, models and notebooks reach only Unity Catalog recipients.

Sharing Recipients.note: Databricks-to-Databricks recipients use a sharing identifier, while other platforms need bearer-token credentials or OIDC federation.

Data Products.note: Domains are a curation layer over existing Unity Catalog assets backed by governed tags; an asset can appear in several domains and grants still gate query access.

Managed ELT.note: Partner ELT is billed separately per connector or row, and Lakeflow Connect now offers managed connectors for many of the same sources inside Unity Catalog.

Custom ETL Tool.note: Hand-written ingestion has to handle schema drift, incremental state and retries itself; Auto Loader supplies file discovery and checkpointing without a managed pipeline.

Streaming Brokers.note: Broker retention caps how far a stream can replay, so a checkpoint older than the retention window forces a backfill from another source.

videos.t: Airline Customer Segmentation with Paul Balm (Amadeus IT Group)

Customer Segmentation.note: Segments are only as stable as the promotion and transaction features behind them, so cluster designs need periodic re-fitting as purchase behaviour drifts.

Churn & Retention.note: Non-contractual businesses have no explicit churn event, so you must define a censoring rule first; survival analysis handles that better than binary classification.

Fraud & Financial Crime.note: Auditors require explainable decisions, so production designs keep the existing rules engine and add model scores alongside it rather than replacing it.

Demand Forecasting.note: Store-item forecasting trains one model per series through pandas UDFs, so compute cost scales with the number of series rather than total data volume.

Personalisation.note: Model choice depends on the situation: content-based or LLM approaches cover cold-start items, while collaborative filtering needs sufficient interaction history.

Customer Service Agents.note: Agents inherit the caller identity through on-behalf-of tokens, so retrieval is already filtered to what that user may read and no separate ACL layer is needed.

Embedded Analytics.note: Only published dashboards can be embedded; external viewers authenticate via a service principal, and with shared data permissions the publisher grants apply instead.

demos.t: Empowering Decisions Through Embedded Analytics with Databricks AI/BI

Feature Store.note: Point-in-time joins and lineage come from registering feature tables in Unity Catalog; online serving is a separate provisioned surface, so a feature is only low-latency once it is published to it.

AI Functions.note: Calls are billed as model inference on top of warehouse compute, and throughput is bounded by the endpoint behind the function, so large batch jobs need a provisioned or batch endpoint rather than pay-per-token.

Agent Mode.note: Renamed from Research Agent. Outside the Americas, Europe, Australia, New Zealand and Japan it runs only where cross-Geo processing is enabled.
